questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis for 10 days. On examination, the ulcer has indurated edges, a clean base and is non-tender. Inguinal lymph nodes are firm and non-tender. Which investigation will give the fastest definitive diagnosis?
opts: Dark-field microscopy of exudate from the ulcer
Tzanck smear from the ulcer base
questions.exp: Dark-field microscopy of ulcer exudate allows direct visualisation of Treponema pallidum spirochetes and is the fastest method for diagnosing primary syphilis. VDRL and FTA-ABS are serological tests that may be negative in early primary syphilis.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman with a butterfly rash, photosensitivity, and joint pains has a renal biopsy showing mesangial deposits. ANA is positive at 1:320 with anti-dsDNA antibodies elevated. She is started on hydroxychloroquine. What is the most important baseline investigation before initiating hydroxychloroquine?
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine can cause irreversible bull's-eye maculopathy leading to permanent vision loss. Baseline ophthalmological evaluation (visual acuity, fundoscopy, visual fields) is mandatory before starting treatment and annually thereafter.

questions.q: A 22-year-old man from a rural area presents with hypopigmented patches on the trunk with loss of sensation. Slit-skin smear shows AFB with Bacterial Index (BI) of 2+. According to WHO classification, this patient has:
opts: Paucibacillary leprosy — treated with 6 months MDT
Multibacillary leprosy — treated with 12 months MDT
Indeterminate leprosy — treated with dapsone monotherapy
questions.exp: A positive slit-skin smear (BI ≥1+) at any site classifies the patient as multibacillary (MB) leprosy, regardless of the number of skin lesions. WHO recommends 12 months MDT (rifampicin + dapsone + clofazimine) for MB leprosy.

questions.q: A 45-year-old diabetic patient presents with rapidly spreading necrotic skin overlying the scrotum and perineum with crepitus on palpation. Blood cultures grow mixed anaerobes and gram-negative organisms. What is the MOST critical initial management?
opts: Immediate aggressive surgical debridement along with IV antibiotics
questions.exp: Fournier's gangrene is a type I necrotising fasciitis of the perineum/scrotum. Mortality is high and the cornerstone of management is immediate aggressive surgical debridement combined with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. Delay in surgery significantly worsens prognosis.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on normal-appearing skin and mucous membrane involvement. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) shows linear IgG and C3 deposits at the dermoepidermal junction. Which diagnosis is most consistent?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid shows linear IgG and C3 deposits along the basement membrane zone on DIF. It typically presents with tense bullae on normal or erythematous skin. Mucous membrane involvement occurs but is less severe than pemphigus. The target antigen is BP180 (collagen XVII).

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with rolled borders, telangiectasia, and central crusting on his nose for 8 months. Histopathology shows palisading tumour cells with peripheral clefting. Which of the following is the treatment of choice for a recurrent lesion at this site?
questions.exp: This describes a nodular basal cell carcinoma (BCC). Mohs micrographic surgery is the gold standard for recurrent BCCs and those in high-risk areas (H-zone of the face including nose, nasolabial fold, periocular area) due to highest cure rates and maximal tissue conservation.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with honey-crusted lesions around the mouth and nose. Culture grows Staphylococcus aureus. The child's sibling is also affected. What is the FIRST-LINE treatment for localised impetigo?
opts: Topical fusidic acid plus oral amoxicillin
questions.exp: Topical mupirocin 2% (or retapamulin) is the first-line treatment for localised non-bullous impetigo. Systemic antibiotics are reserved for widespread lesions, bullous impetigo, or ecthyma. Mupirocin is active against both S. aureus and S. pyogenes.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the lateral aspect of her foot, associated with burning pain. She had a similar episode 4 months ago. The most likely organism is Herpes simplex virus. To prevent recurrences (>6 episodes/year), what is the recommended therapy?
opts: Acyclovir 200 mg five times daily during outbreaks only
Acyclovir 400 mg twice daily as daily suppressive therapy
Valacyclovir 2 g twice daily for one day during outbreaks
Famciclovir 500 mg once daily for 7 days during outbreaks
questions.exp: For frequent recurrences (≥6 per year), daily suppressive therapy with acyclovir 400 mg twice daily (or valacyclovir 500 mg once daily) reduces recurrence frequency by 70-80%. Suppressive therapy is continued for at least 1 year before reassessment.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male presents with well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery white scales on the elbows, knees, and scalp. He also has pitting and onycholysis of fingernails. Which of the following findings on the Auspitz sign correctly describes the pathological basis?
opts: Pinpoint bleeding due to dilation of suprapapillary capillaries after scale removal
Blistering due to acantholysis when lateral pressure is applied
Perilesional erythema after gentle rubbing of lesions
Nikolsky sign positivity reflecting stratum corneum fragility
questions.exp: Auspitz sign in psoriasis refers to pinpoint bleeding spots (blood-stained dew drops) seen after removal of scales. This occurs because psoriatic plaques have dilated tortuous capillaries in elongated dermal papillae, which bleed when the thin suprapapillary epidermis is removed.

questions.q: A 28-year-old HIV-positive man with CD4 count of 80 cells/µL presents with white plaques on the lateral borders of the tongue that cannot be scraped off. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Oral hairy leukoplakia caused by Epstein-Barr virus
Lichen planus of the oral mucosa
questions.exp: Oral hairy leukoplakia (OHL) is caused by EBV and characteristically appears as white corrugated plaques on the lateral borders of the tongue that cannot be scraped off, distinguishing it from candidiasis. It is an AIDS-defining illness seen with severe immunosuppression (CD4 < 200 cells/µL).

questions.q: A patient with leprosy on dapsone treatment develops sudden-onset anaemia, jaundice, and dark urine. Peripheral smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies. Which enzyme deficiency predisposed this patient to this complication?
questions.exp: Dapsone causes oxidative haemolysis, which is markedly exacerbated in patients with G6PD deficiency. G6PD-deficient red cells cannot regenerate NADPH to counter oxidative stress, leading to Heinz body formation, hemolysis (bite cells), jaundice, and haemoglobinuria. G6PD testing is recommended before initiating dapsone.

questions.q: A 32-year-old immunocompetent woman presents with painful grouped vesicles along a dermatome on the right thorax that does not cross the midline. She also has low-grade fever and malaise. The pathophysiology involves reactivation of latent virus in:
opts: Epidermis at the site of primary infection
questions.exp: Herpes zoster (shingles) results from reactivation of Varicella zoster virus (VZV) that has been latent in dorsal root ganglion (DRG) sensory neurons since primary chickenpox infection. Declining cell-mediated immunity allows viral reactivation, with anterograde spread along sensory nerve fibres.

questions.q: A 20-year-old man presents with painful genital ulcers and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy with buboes that are fluctuant. He has multiple sexual partners. Urethral swab Gram stain shows intracellular Gram-negative diplococci in some cells but Donovan bodies are absent. Tzanck test is negative. Which organism is most likely responsible for the painful bubo?
questions.exp: Chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi presents with one or more painful, soft, ragged genital ulcers and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy that can suppurate into buboes. Unlike syphilis (painless ulcer) and LGV (painless ulcer with later bubo), chancroid ulcers are characteristically painful from the onset.

questions.q: A 50-year-old patient is diagnosed with tinea unguium (dermatophyte onychomycosis) affecting 8 fingernails. KOH examination confirms the diagnosis. What is the most appropriate systemic antifungal treatment?
opts: Terbinafine 250 mg daily for 6 weeks (fingernails) or 12 weeks (toenails)
Itraconazole pulse therapy: 400 mg/day for 1 week per month for 2 months
questions.exp: Terbinafine is fungicidal and the drug of choice for dermatophyte onychomycosis. The standard regimen is 250 mg daily for 6 weeks for fingernails and 12 weeks for toenails. Itraconazole pulse therapy is an alternative. Fluconazole is less effective for dermatophytes.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman on long-term methotrexate for psoriasis presents with increasing dyspnoea and dry cough. Chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Pulmonary function tests show restrictive pattern. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Methotrexate pneumonitis is an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reaction (not dose-dependent) that can occur at any time during therapy. It presents with dry cough, dyspnoea, and bilateral interstitial infiltrates on CXR with restrictive spirometry. Management includes immediate cessation of methotrexate and systemic corticosteroids.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with symmetric hyperpigmented patches on the cheeks, upper lip, and forehead, worsening in summer. She is on oral contraceptive pills. Wood's lamp examination accentuates the hyperpigmentation. What does Wood's lamp accentuation indicate?
opts: Dermal melanin deposition — poor prognosis for treatment
Epidermal melanin deposition — relatively good prognosis for treatment
questions.exp: In melasma, Wood's lamp (365 nm UV light) accentuates pigmentation when melanin is primarily in the epidermis (epidermal type), as melanin in the epidermis absorbs UV more efficiently. Epidermal melasma responds better to depigmenting agents (hydroquinone, kojic acid, azelaic acid) compared to dermal type.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child has intensely pruritic papules and vesicles between the fingers, on the wrists, axillae, and genitalia. The mother has similar symptoms. Dermoscopy reveals jet-ski/motorboat-like structures (burrows) with a small dark oval at one end. What is the diagnostic organism and its lifecycle feature of significance?
opts: Pediculus humanus — lays nits attached to hair shafts
Sarcoptes scabiei — female mite burrows into stratum corneum to lay eggs
Phthirus pubis — grasps hair shafts with claw-like legs
questions.exp: Scabies is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. The fertilised female mite burrows into the stratum corneum and lays 2-3 eggs daily. The burrow is the pathognomonic lesion. Dermoscopy shows the 'delta-wing jet sign' — the dark triangular mite at the end of the burrow. Permethrin 5% cream is first-line treatment.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man underwent punch biopsy for a suspected melanocytic lesion. Histopathology shows a lesion with irregular nests of melanocytes at the DEJ, pagetoid spread, nuclear atypia, and solar elastosis in the adjacent dermis. What is the MOST important prognostic factor for this melanoma?
opts: Breslow thickness (depth of invasion in millimetres)
Number of mitoses per high-power field
questions.exp: Breslow thickness (the vertical depth of melanoma invasion measured in millimetres from the granular layer of the epidermis to the deepest tumour cell) is the single most important prognostic factor for primary cutaneous melanoma. It determines T staging in the AJCC TNM classification and guides surgical margins.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with fragile blisters and erosions on the face and upper trunk. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows intercellular 'chicken-wire' or 'fishnet' IgG deposits in the epidermis. Which antigen is targeted by the pathological autoantibodies?
opts: Type VII collagen in anchoring fibrils
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) is caused by IgG autoantibodies primarily targeting Desmoglein 3 (and in mucocutaneous involvement, also Dsg1). Dsg3 is critical for keratinocyte adhesion. Loss of Dsg3 function causes intraepidermal acantholysis (suprabasal split), resulting in flaccid blisters and positive Nikolsky sign.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of painless ulcers on the genitals with beefy red granulation tissue and raised edges. Smear from the lesion shows large mononuclear cells with intracytoplasmic rod-shaped bacteria (Donovan bodies). What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for at least 3 weeks
Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days
questions.exp: Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly Calymmatobacterium granulomatis). Donovan bodies are the pathognomonic finding on Giemsa or Wright's stain. Doxycycline 100 mg BD for minimum 3 weeks (until lesions heal) is the CDC-recommended first-line therapy.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man presents with a firm, skin-coloured to pinkish nodule on the dorsum of his right hand for 2 years. Dermoscopy shows a white 'chrysalis-like' structure and a central white scar. Histopathology reveals a spindle-cell proliferation in a storiform pattern with trapped collagen bundles at the periphery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Dermatofibroma (benign fibrous histiocytoma) classically shows a positive dimple (Fitzpatrick) sign — it dimples inward when pinched laterally, unlike DFSP. Histology shows storiform spindle cells entrapping collagen bundles ('collagen trapping') at the periphery. Dermoscopy may reveal a peripheral white ring and central scar-like area.

questions.q: A 19-year-old woman presents with multiple comedones, inflammatory papules, pustules, and a few nodules on her face and back. She has tried topical retinoids and benzoyl peroxide for 6 months with inadequate response. What is the indication threshold for starting oral isotretinoin?
opts: Presence of more than 20 comedones despite topical treatment
Severe nodulo-cystic acne, acne unresponsive to conventional therapy, acne causing scarring, or acne with significant psychosocial impact
Acne during pregnancy in any severity
questions.exp: Oral isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid) is indicated for: severe nodulo-cystic/conglobate acne, acne resistant to conventional therapy (antibiotics + topicals), acne with scarring tendency, acne with significant psychological impact, and recurrent severe acne. It is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogen — iPLEDGE programme in USA).

questions.q: A 50-year-old female patient presents with 6-month history of diffuse hair loss predominantly from the crown of the scalp with preservation of the frontal hairline. Dermatoscopy shows peripilar signs (brown halos) and yellow dots. Scalp biopsy shows miniaturisation of follicles with increased telogen:anagen ratio. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.exp: Female pattern hair loss (FPHL/androgenetic alopecia) shows characteristic Ludwig pattern distribution. First-line treatment in women is topical minoxidil (2% or 5%). Minoxidil prolongs anagen phase and increases follicle size. Oral finasteride is used off-label in post-menopausal women but is teratogenic and not recommended in pre-menopausal women without strict contraception.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer presents with painless subcutaneous swellings on the foot and ankle with multiple draining sinuses discharging black granules. X-ray shows 'punched-out' osteolytic lesions. What is the most appropriate systemic treatment for actinomycetoma?
questions.exp: Mycetoma caused by actinomycetes (actinomycetoma — Nocardia, Actinomadura, Streptomyces species) is bacterial and responds to antibiotics. First-line regimens include high-dose co-trimoxazole alone or combined with other antibiotics (rifampicin, amikacin). Eumycetoma (fungal) is treated with itraconazole or voriconazole.

questions.q: A 27-year-old woman presents with erythema, oedema, vesicles, and intense pruritus on the dorsum of her hands and wrists after wearing a new metal watch. Patch testing shows a positive reaction to nickel sulphate. This is an example of which immunological mechanism?
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is a classic example of Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity. It is T-cell-mediated, occurring in two phases: sensitisation (first exposure, no reaction) and elicitation (subsequent exposure, reaction peaks at 48-96 hours). Nickel is the most common contact allergen worldwide.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man with extensive psoriasis involving >30% BSA has failed methotrexate and cyclosporine. He is started on adalimumab, a TNF-alpha inhibitor. Before initiating biological therapy, which screening test is MANDATORY?
opts: Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) or IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold) for latent TB
questions.exp: TNF-alpha plays a crucial role in granuloma formation that contains latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab) can reactivate latent TB, leading to disseminated or extrapulmonary TB. Mandatory screening for latent TB (Mantoux/IGRA + chest X-ray) before initiating any TNF inhibitor is essential.

questions.q: A 2-year-old child presents with grouped vesicles on the trunk with positive Nikolsky sign. The child had fever 3 days ago and now has large flaccid bullae. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus phage group II. What toxin is responsible for the skin findings?
opts: Exfoliative toxin A and B (ET-A, ET-B) targeting desmoglein-1
Alpha toxin causing direct membrane damage
questions.exp: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is caused by exfoliative toxins A and B (serine proteases) produced by S. aureus phage group II. These toxins specifically cleave desmoglein-1 (Dsg1) in the superficial epidermis (granular layer), causing intraepidermal cleavage and superficial blistering/desquamation.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with thickened skin, Raynaud's phenomenon, dysphagia, telangiectasias, and calcinosis cutis. She has anti-centromere antibodies. Which diagnosis does she have?
opts: Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc) — CREST syndrome
questions.exp: The described features — Calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, oEsophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias — constitute CREST syndrome, which is the classic presentation of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc). Anti-centromere antibodies are the characteristic autoantibody in lcSSc, present in ~70-80% of cases.

questions.q: A 48-year-old man presents with chronic itching and burning in the perianal region. Examination reveals well-defined white plaques with a 'cigarette paper' surface texture involving the perianal skin, scrotum, and extending to the glans penis. Biopsy shows epidermal atrophy with basal cell vacuolisation and homogenised dermis. What is the risk associated with this condition if untreated?
opts: Risk of squamous cell carcinoma (~4-6%) — especially on mucosal surfaces
Risk of basal cell carcinoma only
questions.exp: Lichen sclerosus et atrophicus (LSA) presenting with the described features has a ~4-6% risk of malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), particularly in genital lesions in both males and females. Regular surveillance is mandatory. First-line treatment is ultra-potent topical corticosteroids (clobetasol propionate 0.05%).

questions.q: A 22-year-old medical student performs a photopatch test. Which of the following disorders is BEST diagnosed with this test?
opts: Photoallergic contact dermatitis from topical sunscreens or fragrances
questions.exp: Photopatch testing identifies photoallergic contact dermatitis — a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction requiring both the photosensitising chemical (e.g., benzophenone in sunscreens, NSAID gels) and UV-A irradiation. Duplicate patches are applied: one site is irradiated with UV-A, the other is not. A reaction only at the irradiated site confirms photoallergy.

questions.q: During a dermatological procedure, a clinician injects local anaesthetic around a digital nerve at the base of a finger to achieve anaesthesia for nail surgery. Which local anaesthetic is CONTRAINDICATED for digital nerve blocks?
questions.exp: Lignocaine with adrenaline (epinephrine) is contraindicated in digital nerve blocks. Adrenaline causes vasoconstriction of the digital arteries (end arteries), risking ischaemia and necrosis of the digit. Plain lignocaine, bupivacaine, or ropivacaine without vasoconstrictors are safe alternatives for ring/digital blocks.
